sysd-blocks-188.q: What happens in a B-tree when a key is inserted into a leaf that is already full, and what if the split reaches the root?
sysd-blocks-188.a: The leaf is split into two around a median key, which moves up to the parent as a separation value; a split that reaches the root creates a new root and increases the tree's height.

sysd-blocks-091.q: Why does an index on (ID, Name) let a query for a record's Name skip the table lookup, and what does that cost?
sysd-blocks-091.a: A covering index holds the needed fields itself, so the index alone answers the query and the record lookup disappears; the cost is a larger index, because the extra keys slow down inserts and updates.

sysd-blocks-092.q: How do pessimistic and optimistic locking differ in handling conflicts, and which favors data integrity?
sysd-blocks-092.a: Pessimistic locking locks the data before any change and blocks other users, which is better for data integrity but can hurt performance; optimistic locking lets many users in, checks for conflicts at commit and rolls back if one is found, which is better for efficiency and performance.

sysd-blocks-086.q: Why does a search on city and first_name use only the city part of an index on (city, last_name, first_name)?
sysd-blocks-086.a: Only the first indexed column can be used on its own, so the search uses city and then checks first_name sequentially; creating the index in the order of the search columns avoids this.

sysd-blocks-096.q: Why is 6NF unsuitable for databases serving online transaction processing?
sysd-blocks-096.a: Its drawback is a proliferation of tables: a 5NF table with one key column and N attributes needs N tables, so multi-field updates, inserts and deletes touch several tables.

sysd-blocks-199.q: Why can't SRAM, though much faster than DRAM, match DRAM's storage capacity?
sysd-blocks-199.a: Each SRAM bit takes a cell of six transistors, whereas DRAM needs only one capacitor and one transistor per bit, which makes DRAM space-efficient and inexpensive.

sysd-blocks-210.q: Why must a database flush its log to non-volatile storage before acknowledging a commit?
sysd-blocks-210.a: So that the effects of committed transactions survive the loss of volatile memory: because changes are logged before they modify database state, committed transactions can be redone from the log after a crash and incomplete ones undone, recreating the state right before the failure.

sysd-blocks-200.q: Which kind of storage is fully owned by a single server, and why do databases and virtual machine engines still want it?
sysd-blocks-200.a: Block storage: it is the most flexible and versatile form, so databases and virtual machine engines manage blocks directly to squeeze out the most performance, but it is fully owned by a single server and is not a shared resource.

sysd-blocks-149.q: What does data scrubbing do in a RAID array, and why does it reduce risk during a rebuild?
sysd-blocks-149.a: The controller periodically reads and checks all blocks, including those not otherwise accessed, and uses the array's redundancy to recover a bad block and reassign it to spare blocks; this catches unrecoverable read errors early, reducing the risk of double-drive failures during a rebuild.

sysd-blocks-156.q: Why is object storage not suited to transactional data?
sysd-blocks-156.a: It lacks the locking and sharing mechanisms that keep a single, accurately updated version of a file; it deliberately trades performance for high durability, vast scale and low cost, and targets relatively cold data such as archives and backups.

sysd-blocks-147.q: How does network-attached storage differ from direct-attached storage?
sysd-blocks-147.a: Direct-attached storage is traditional mass storage that uses no network, while network-attached storage is accessed by another computer at file level over a local or wide area network or the Internet, commonly using the Network File System and Server Message Block protocols.

sysd-blocks-207.q: Why does SMB2 perform better than SMB 1.0 over high-latency links?
sysd-blocks-207.a: SMB 1.0 is chatty, block-level and limited to a 64K block size; SMB2 cuts the commands from over a hundred to nineteen, pipelines requests before earlier responses arrive, and compounds multiple actions into one request to save round trips.

sysd-blocks-198.q: Why does an SSD controller do wear leveling, and what does it cost?
sysd-blocks-198.a: Without it, specific blocks would wear out early from repeated use and shorten the life of the whole drive; the controller moves cold data off heavily used blocks so hot data can be written there, and the extra writes, called write amplification, must be balanced against performance and durability.

sysd-blocks-203.q: How do object stores differ from key-value stores?
sysd-blocks-203.a: Object stores associate a limited set of attributes (metadata) with each piece of data, are optimized for hundreds of megabytes or even gigabytes and usually offer weaker consistency such as eventual consistency; key-value stores expect small values (kilobytes) and offer strong consistency.

sysd-blocks-148.q: How does 4 + 2 erasure coding compare with 3-copy replication on storage overhead and durability?
sysd-blocks-148.a: In 4 + 2 erasure coding every two chunks of data need one parity block, so the storage overhead is 50% against 200% for 3-copy replication; Backblaze's calculation, assuming a 0.81% annual node failure rate, gives 11 nines of durability against 6 nines.

sysd-blocks-153.q: A highly available design adds redundant components. Why must it also provide reliable crossover?
sysd-blocks-153.a: In redundant systems the crossover point itself tends to become a single point of failure, so reliable systems must provide for reliable crossover.

sysd-scale-073.q: What is the chance that a system survives to its MTBF, and why does it matter?
sysd-scale-073.a: About 37% (1/e), not the 50% many engineers assume, and that misreading can lead to bad design decisions.

sysd-scale-136.q: Why does speeding up one part of a system by a huge factor often barely help overall?
sysd-scale-136.a: The overall gain is limited by the fraction of time that part is actually used: speeding up a part that takes 10% of execution time by a factor of 10,000 gives an overall speedup of only 1.11, an 11% improvement.

sysd-scale-066.q: What do contention and coherency mean in the Universal Scalability Law, and what does high contention suggest?
sysd-scale-066.a: Contention is delay from waiting or queueing for shared resources, and coherence is delay for data to become consistent; high contention indicates sequential processing that could be parallelized, while high coherency suggests excessive dependencies among processes.

sysd-scale-067.q: How can a site claim very high availability while its service goes down for maintenance?
sysd-scale-067.a: Many sites exclude scheduled downtime from their availability calculations, but for true high availability downtime is downtime whether or not it is scheduled.

sysd-scale-134.q: A system stays up all year but suffers a 9-hour network failure at peak usage. Is it 100% available?
sysd-scale-134.a: No: users see it as unavailable even though the administrator claims 100% uptime. By the true definition it is approximately 99.9% available, three nines: 8751 hours of available time out of 8760 hours.

sysd-scale-076.q: Why does chaining two 99.9%-available components lower availability, while running them in parallel raises it?
sysd-scale-076.a: In sequence, total availability is the product of the components' availabilities, so two at 99.9% each give 99.8%; in parallel it is 1 minus the product of their unavailabilities, so two at 99.9% each give 99.9999%.

sysd-scale-063.q: Why can't replication stand in for a backup?
sysd-scale-063.a: A backup copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.

sysd-scale-058.q: Why does a gossip protocol keep spreading information even when some messages are lost?
sysd-scale-058.a: Each node periodically picks another node at random and shares what it knows, so a rumor roughly doubles its reach each round, and that doubling keeps the protocol robust even when some messages are lost.

sysd-scale-131.q: Why can no deterministic algorithm elect a leader in an anonymous ring?
sysd-scale-131.a: All the processes are identical and run at the same speed, so symmetry cannot be broken; randomized algorithms can pick a leader with high probability.

sysd-scale-046.q: What happens if one record is changed on two nodes at once under eager versus lazy multi-master replication?
sysd-scale-046.a: An eager system detects the conflict before confirming the commit and aborts one transaction; a lazy system lets both commit and resolves the conflict during re-synchronization.

sysd-scale-122.q: Why does requiring Vr + Vw > V guarantee that a read sees the newest version?
sysd-scale-122.a: Because the read and write quorum votes together must exceed the total votes, every read quorum overlaps every write quorum and so includes the newest version, with version numbers showing which copies are current.

sysd-scale-048.q: How can a system keep a user from missing an order they just placed when a replica lags behind the primary?
sysd-scale-048.a: Send latency-sensitive reads, and reads that immediately follow writes, to the primary database; or check whether the replica has caught up with the primary and, if not, fail the read or read from the primary.

sysd-scale-132.q: How does PostgreSQL logical replication start replicating a table and keep its changes consistent?
sysd-scale-132.a: A snapshot of the table is copied to the subscriber first, then changes made since the copy are sent continually and applied in the publisher's order, so transactional consistency holds within one subscription.

sysd-scale-130.q: What happens if every heartbeat link between cluster nodes fails while the nodes keep running?
sysd-scale-130.a: Each node believes it is the only one running, so each serves clients from its own data set with no coordination, which can corrupt data or cause inconsistencies that need operator cleanup.

sysd-scale-126.q: A G-Counter can only increment. How does a PN-Counter support decrements?
sysd-scale-126.a: It combines two G-Counters, one counting increments and one counting decrements, and its value is the increment total minus the decrement total.

sysd-scale-082.q: How does round-robin partitioning place rows, and what is its drawback?
sysd-scale-082.a: It sends the ith tuple in insertion order to partition (i mod n), giving uniform distribution and parallel sequential access, but reaching tuples by a predicate means accessing the entire relation.

sysd-scale-087.q: Why do timestamp keys pile writes onto one partition in a sensor network, and how does a compound key help?
sysd-scale-087.a: With timestamp keys, writes concentrate in the partition of the current time period; prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load.

sysd-scale-088.q: Why does shard_id = hash(user_id) % num_shards make adding database servers expensive, and what fixes it?
sysd-scale-088.a: Changing the number of slots remaps nearly all keys, so adding or removing servers is expensive; consistent hashing, which hashes keys and servers onto a circle, fixes this by moving only the keys next to the changed server, a 1/n fraction when adding the nth server.

sysd-scale-139.q: Why do virtual nodes spread load more evenly after a server fails?
sysd-scale-139.a: Without them a failed server's keys all move to the next server clockwise, potentially doubling its load; with several positions per server, its keys are reassigned to different servers, spreading them more evenly.

sysd-scale-140.q: Why should a table be optimized locally before it is sharded?
sysd-scale-140.a: Sharding is generally recommended only when other optimization strategies have proven insufficient, and sharding a table before it has been optimized locally adds needless complexity.

sysd-scale-092.q: Why is eventual consistency only a liveness guarantee and not a safety one?
sysd-scale-092.a: It promises only that reads eventually return the same value, with no safety guarantee, so any intermediate value is allowed before convergence.

sysd-scale-107.q: What trade-off does PACELC add to CAP that applies even when there is no partition?
sysd-scale-107.a: Latency versus consistency: consistent operations need a full network round trip on reads and writes, so low-latency systems relax consistency to reduce delay. CAP matters only during a partition, but this trade-off is present at all times.

sysd-scale-099.q: What part of the design space does CAP actually rule out?
sysd-scale-099.a: Only a tiny part: perfect availability and consistency in the presence of partitions, which are rare. Designers need to sacrifice consistency or availability only when a partition is present.
